items.prompt: A new regional workload will create thousands of resources during a launch event. What should the architect do before the event?
constraints: The launch date is fixed.
The workload uses several regional AWS services.
A quota increase might require lead time.

options.text: Inventory the service quotas in the target Region, compare them with peak demand and failover demand, request increases where needed, and test the resulting limits.
Assume managed services automatically raise every quota when traffic increases.
Increase instance sizes so account-level quotas no longer apply.
Wait for launch-day throttling and then open a support case.

feedback.Reason: Quotas are design constraints that must be checked against normal and recovery demand before the workload is exposed to a launch surge.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Service Quotas exposes adjustable and non-adjustable limits by account and Region, and quota requests can require planning time.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect models steady state, burst, and failover consumption and validates the requested quota increases in the deployment Region.
Details.errorCorrection: Managed-service operation does not remove account or regional quotas, and instance size does not eliminate service-level limits.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Requesting excess quota does not create capacity or remove downstream bottlenecks; the design still needs load testing and headroom.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Quotas are not universally raised automatically when demand grows.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Changing instance size does not change quotas for APIs, resources, or account usage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Waiting moves a predictable launch risk into production.

items.prompt: An API client receives intermittent 429 responses during bursts, although the backend is healthy. Which client behavior is the best first correction?
constraints: Requests are safe to retry.
The API has a documented throttle limit.
Many clients retry at the same time.

options.text: Retry immediately in a tight loop until a request succeeds.
Use bounded exponential backoff with jitter, honor retry guidance, and control client concurrency.
Disable retries and discard every throttled request.
Add an unrelated NAT gateway because throttling is always a network translation failure.

feedback.Reason: Backoff with jitter reduces synchronized retry storms while bounded retries preserve a defined failure outcome.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Exponential delay spreads retries over time and jitter prevents clients from retrying in lockstep against the same quota.
Details.scenarioApplication: The client treats 429 as a capacity signal, limits in-flight work, and retries only idempotent operations within a deadline.
Details.errorCorrection: A tight loop amplifies throttling, while discarding all requests loses recoverable work and a NAT gateway does not raise an API quota.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backoff increases latency and requires a dead-letter or error path when the retry budget is exhausted.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Immediate retries increase pressure on the already-throttled API.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Permanent discard is not appropriate for safely retryable work.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: API throttling and NAT capacity are different constraints.

items.prompt: A worker fleet is hitting Amazon SQS API request quotas even though the number of messages is moderate. Which change reduces request pressure without losing messages?
constraints: The worker can process multiple messages together.
At-least-once processing is acceptable.
Visibility timeout is already sized for the batch.

options.text: Use ReceiveMessage and DeleteMessageBatch where appropriate, and tune long polling and worker concurrency.
Poll more frequently with a shorter wait time so quota use is more predictable.
Create a new queue for every worker thread without changing polling behavior.
Delete messages individually before processing them.

feedback.Reason: Batch APIs and long polling reduce unnecessary request volume while preserving the queue's delivery contract.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: SQS supports batching and long polling so a worker can receive more useful work per API request and avoid empty polls.
Details.scenarioApplication: Workers receive batches, process each message idempotently, and delete only successfully processed messages in a batch.
Details.errorCorrection: More short polls consume quota, queue proliferation does not remove the per-account or per-API constraint, and early deletion risks loss.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Batches can increase per-message latency or retry granularity, so visibility and partial-batch failure handling must be designed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Short polling and more frequent calls increase request usage.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: More queues add operational complexity and do not fix an inefficient poller.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Deleting before successful processing can lose work.

items.prompt: A critical Lambda function must always retain capacity, while a batch function must not consume all account concurrency. Which design addresses both requirements?
constraints: The critical function has a known peak concurrency.
The batch function is bursty.
The account concurrency quota is finite.

options.text: Give both functions unbounded concurrency and rely on downstream errors to regulate them.
Increase function memory only; memory allocation reserves concurrency automatically.
Reserve concurrency for the critical function and cap the batch function, then request account quota or redesign if aggregate demand exceeds it.
Put both functions in one VPC subnet to share concurrency safely.

feedback.Reason: Reserved and maximum concurrency partition a finite account capacity so one workload cannot starve another.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Lambda concurrency settings can reserve capacity for a function and cap another function's concurrency; account quota remains the aggregate ceiling.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect sizes reservations from peak demand, caps batch work, and verifies that the total required concurrency fits the account quota.
Details.errorCorrection: Memory changes execution resources, not the account concurrency ceiling, and a subnet does not partition Lambda concurrency.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Over-reservation can strand capacity and lower burst flexibility, so reservations need evidence and periodic review.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Unbounded callers can let batch work starve the critical function.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Memory size and concurrency quota are separate controls.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: VPC placement does not control Lambda concurrency allocation.

items.prompt: An Auto Scaling group can launch enough instances for normal traffic, but a Region failover would exceed the account's EC2 On-Demand vCPU quota. What is the best correction?
constraints: The failover Region uses the same instance family.
The recovery plan requires immediate scale-out.
The quota is adjustable.

options.text: Request a sufficient regional vCPU quota increase, validate it before the incident, and retain capacity headroom for failover.
Set the Auto Scaling maximum above the quota and assume the group will bypass the limit.
Disable health checks during failover so fewer instances are needed.
Move the launch template to a different Availability Zone in the same Region.

feedback.Reason: Recovery capacity is not real capacity if the account quota prevents the recovery fleet from launching.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: EC2 On-Demand Instance quotas are regional and constrain aggregate vCPU usage for the relevant instance families.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team requests and confirms the quota, models normal plus failover usage, and sets scaling limits below an operationally safe ceiling.
Details.errorCorrection: An Auto Scaling maximum cannot override a service quota, and changing AZ or health checks does not create vCPU quota.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Quota increases do not guarantee physical capacity, so launch diversity, capacity reservations, and tested recovery remain relevant.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Auto Scaling remains subject to the regional quota.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Disabling health checks weakens recovery and does not increase launch quota.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Availability Zones share the regional account quota.

items.prompt: Private instances open many short-lived connections to one public destination and begin failing intermittently. Which investigation and design response is most appropriate?
constraints: The instances use a NAT gateway for egress.
The destination and application are healthy.
Failures correlate with connection bursts.

options.text: Increase the subnet CIDR only; NAT connection limits are determined by the source subnet address count.
Inspect NAT gateway connection and port behavior, reduce connection churn with pooling, and distribute egress across gateways or destinations when justified.
Disable security groups so ephemeral ports are never exhausted.
Add an Internet gateway route to the private subnet while keeping the instances private.

feedback.Reason: NAT gateway connection and port behavior can become a capacity boundary for bursty egress, especially when many flows target one destination.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Connection reuse reduces ephemeral-port churn, while deliberate egress distribution can increase available connection capacity and isolate faults.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team measures active connections and errors, pools connections, and scales the egress path based on observed demand rather than changing unrelated routing.
Details.errorCorrection: A larger CIDR does not automatically remove a NAT port boundary, security groups do not create ports, and an Internet gateway does not make a private subnet's instances public safely.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More NAT gateways add cost and routing complexity, so the design should first fix connection churn and validate need.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Subnet address space is not the direct control for a destination connection limit.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Security groups do not cause the NAT gateway's ephemeral-port capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: An Internet gateway route would not provide the intended private egress design.

items.prompt: A DynamoDB table with provisioned capacity throttles during a predictable daily spike. Which change best addresses the known pattern?
constraints: The access pattern is valid and partitioned.
The spike can be forecast.
The team wants to preserve availability during the spike.

options.text: Use Application Auto Scaling or on-demand capacity as appropriate, monitor consumed versus provisioned capacity, and validate partition behavior.
Add a global secondary index for every attribute so the base table receives more write capacity.
Lower provisioned capacity so DynamoDB will stop throttling requests.
Put the table behind a NAT gateway to increase write throughput.

feedback.Reason: Capacity mode and autoscaling should match the workload's variability, while partition behavior must be checked separately from aggregate capacity.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: DynamoDB provisioned capacity can be adjusted with Application Auto Scaling, and on-demand capacity handles variable traffic without manual provisioning.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect selects the mode from demand shape, sets safe scaling boundaries, and checks for hot partitions rather than treating every throttle as an account quota.
Details.errorCorrection: Extra indexes can add write work, lowering capacity worsens throttling, and NAT is unrelated to DynamoDB service capacity.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Autoscaling has reaction time and on-demand pricing differs, so a forecasted spike may need scheduled capacity or pre-warming.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Indexes generally add capacity consumption; they do not fix a base-table throttle.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Lower capacity makes throttling more likely.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: NAT connectivity does not increase DynamoDB write capacity.

items.prompt: A Kinesis data stream starts returning write-throttling errors when producers exceed the per-shard write rate. What is the correct capacity response?
constraints: The stream's ordering model permits additional shards.
Producer demand is expected to grow.
The consumer can process a larger shard set.

options.text: Increase shard capacity through resharding or an appropriate stream mode, update consumers for the new shard topology, and retain headroom.
Increase only the producer retry count without changing capacity or backoff.
Put all records on one partition key to force Kinesis to balance them.
Replace the stream with an S3 bucket while keeping the real-time consumer contract unchanged.

feedback.Reason: A per-shard throughput limit is addressed by increasing effective shard capacity and ensuring consumers understand the resulting topology.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Kinesis data streams have shard-level read and write limits; resharding or on-demand capacity changes the available throughput.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures per-shard utilization, chooses a scaling operation, and load-tests producer and consumer behavior with a reserve for bursts.
Details.errorCorrection: More retries without backoff amplify throttling, a single partition key concentrates traffic, and S3 does not preserve the same streaming contract.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More shards increase cost and can affect consumer coordination, so partition-key distribution and scaling limits must be reviewed.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Retries cannot create shard throughput and may intensify the overload.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: One key creates a hot shard rather than balancing records.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Changing to S3 changes latency and consumer semantics.

items.prompt: A quota increase request is rejected because the service team cannot determine the intended usage. What evidence should the architect add?
constraints: The requested quota is adjustable.
The workload has measured traffic data.
The target is a specific Region and account.

options.text: Submit only the largest possible number so the account has no future constraint.
Describe the workload, current and forecast peak usage, normal and failover demand, Region, timeline, and the operational controls that prevent runaway usage.
Ask for a quota increase in a different Region because quotas are global.
Remove monitoring so the service sees fewer quota alarms.

feedback.Reason: A quota request is stronger when it shows a bounded, evidence-based capacity need and an operating plan.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Service Quotas requests are scoped to a service and Region and should state the intended usage and requested value.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect attaches observed metrics, growth assumptions, failover calculations, and the launch timeline so the request can be evaluated before production.
Details.errorCorrection: An arbitrary maximum is not a capacity plan, regional quotas are not automatically global, and hiding alarms removes useful evidence.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: An approved quota still needs budget, downstream service capacity, and a review date as demand evolves.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: The largest possible request lacks a reasoned demand model.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Many quotas are regional, so a different Region does not solve the target Region.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Monitoring is evidence and should not be removed.

items.prompt: A single CloudFormation stack is approaching resource and operation limits, making updates slow and fragile. Which architecture improves operability?
constraints: The application has independently deployable tiers.
Cross-stack outputs can be kept stable.
The team wants to retain infrastructure as code.

options.text: Split the stack into coherent nested or independently managed stacks, define stable interfaces, and deploy them with an explicit dependency order.
Copy the same resources into the stack until CloudFormation accepts the template.
Replace CloudFormation with manual console changes so limits no longer apply.
Put all resources in one template and disable rollback.

feedback.Reason: Coherent stack boundaries reduce blast radius and keep each deployment within service limits while preserving declarative ownership.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: CloudFormation has template and stack resource limits; nested stacks and cross-stack references let a large system be decomposed deliberately.
Details.scenarioApplication: Network, shared services, and application layers expose stable outputs and are updated in a controlled dependency order.
Details.errorCorrection: Duplicating resources increases risk, console changes remove the source of truth, and disabling rollback weakens recovery.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: More stacks require interface and lifecycle discipline; decomposition must not create hidden circular dependencies.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Adding resources increases the limit problem and may create duplicates.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Manual changes create drift and do not remove the underlying service limits.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Disabling rollback leaves failed changes harder to recover.

items.prompt: An S3 workload receives occasional 503 Slow Down responses after a traffic pattern change. Which response is most appropriate?
constraints: Objects are accessed through the S3 API.
Operations can be retried safely.
The client currently retries immediately.

options.text: Use exponential backoff with jitter, limit concurrency, and review request distribution and client behavior before changing the data model.
Add random characters to every object key without measuring the client request pattern.
Retry in a tight loop because S3 has unlimited request capacity.
Put S3 behind an RDS Proxy to pool object requests.

feedback.Reason: S3 can scale request rates, but clients still need correct retry behavior and controlled concurrency when they receive Slow Down responses.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: S3 recommends retrying transient errors with exponential backoff and avoiding synchronized request bursts; request patterns should be measured.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team instruments request rates and prefixes, bounds workers, and retries within an application deadline rather than multiplying load.
Details.errorCorrection: Blind key randomization can harm organization and is not a substitute for diagnosis, tight retries amplify load, and RDS Proxy is for database connections.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Backoff may increase latency, and application semantics must decide when work moves to a durable retry path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Changing keys without evidence is not a general correction and may create operational costs.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Tight retries intensify the request burst.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: RDS Proxy does not proxy S3 API calls.

items.prompt: An Auto Scaling group is normally at its desired capacity, but it cannot respond quickly enough to a predictable burst. What should be changed first?
constraints: The burst has a known daily window.
Launching instances takes several minutes.
The workload must remain available during scale-out.

options.text: Lower the minimum capacity to reduce cost and let the group scale from zero during the burst.
Use scheduled or predictive capacity for the known demand and keep minimum and warm headroom sufficient for launch latency.
Increase the health-check grace period until the burst ends.
Scale only from CPU after the burst has already saturated the instances.

feedback.Reason: Headroom must cover the time between demand arrival and new capacity becoming healthy.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Scheduled or predictive scaling can add capacity before a known event, while minimum capacity and warm resources protect the launch interval.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect measures instance launch and health-check time, schedules the burst, and retains enough spare capacity for forecast error.
Details.errorCorrection: Lowering minimum capacity removes resilience, a grace period changes health evaluation rather than capacity, and CPU-only reaction is late for this burst.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Extra capacity costs money and forecasts can be wrong, so schedules should be reviewed against demand evidence.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Scaling from zero increases the period with no serving capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: A grace period does not make instances launch or process requests faster.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: A reactive CPU signal arrives after the burst has caused pressure.

items.prompt: A team wants an alarm for a quota that protects a failover plan. Which threshold is most useful?
constraints: The quota is used by normal and recovery workloads.
Recovery must remain possible during a regional incident.
Usage varies over time.

options.text: Alarm only when the exact quota limit is reached.
Alarm on a sustained utilization level that leaves the modeled failover headroom, with a separate alert for rapid growth or quota changes.
Alarm when usage is zero because zero usage means the quota is unavailable.
Avoid quota alarms because AWS prevents quota exhaustion automatically.

feedback.Reason: A quota alarm must fire before normal consumption removes the capacity required for recovery.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Headroom is the difference between the quota and modeled demand; thresholds should reflect recovery requirements and measurement noise.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner alarms before the failover boundary, links the alert to a quota-increase or load-shedding runbook, and watches the growth trend.
Details.errorCorrection: Waiting for the hard limit is late, zero usage is not exhaustion, and AWS does not guarantee automatic quota increases.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: A low threshold can create noise, so sustained windows and separate rate-of-change alerts are useful.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: At the hard limit, new operations may already be failing.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Zero usage does not indicate quota exhaustion.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Quota exhaustion remains an application and operations responsibility.

items.prompt: A warm-standby Region is sized for recovery, but its account has no unused service quota because the standby is already serving background workloads. What is the key correction?
constraints: The standby must scale during failover.
Background workloads are not business-critical.
The quota applies to the standby Region.

options.text: Treat the standby as available because its resources are in a different Availability Zone.
Remove all monitoring from the background workload so it consumes less quota.
Model both workloads together, reserve or request quota for failover, and define how background work is reduced during recovery.
Assume the primary Region's unused quota is shared automatically with the standby.

feedback.Reason: A standby is only operationally ready when its quota and capacity budget include the recovery workload, not just its steady background load.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Regional quotas constrain the combined usage of workloads in that Region; failover plans need a defined capacity reservation or load-shedding policy.
Details.scenarioApplication: The owner calculates primary recovery demand plus standby demand, obtains quota, and documents which noncritical work yields during recovery.
Details.errorCorrection: AZ separation does not create regional quota, hiding monitoring does not remove usage, and quotas are not pooled between Regions.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Keeping spare quota and capacity costs money, but an untested or quota-starved standby is not a reliable recovery path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: A different AZ still uses the same regional service quota.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Monitoring is not the source of the workload's resource consumption.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Service quotas are generally scoped to the account, service, and Region rather than shared globally.

items.prompt: A service is approaching an API quota and must preserve checkout availability. Which behavior is safest?
constraints: Checkout is more important than reporting.
Requests can be classified by business priority.
The quota cannot be increased before the event.

options.text: Allow all callers to retry indefinitely so no request is rejected.
Apply priority-aware admission control, shed or defer lower-value work, and bound retries so critical requests retain quota.
Return success for every request and process the work only if capacity later becomes available.
Throttle checkout first because it generates the most traffic.

feedback.Reason: Explicit load shedding protects the business-critical path when demand exceeds a finite capacity boundary.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Admission control and bounded retries prevent low-priority traffic from consuming the entire quota and creating a retry storm.
Details.scenarioApplication: The service queues or rejects reporting work with an observable status while preserving checkout requests within a defined deadline.
Details.errorCorrection: Infinite retries worsen overload, false success breaks correctness, and prioritizing the highest-value path for throttling is backwards.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Lower-priority work may be delayed or rejected, so clients need a durable retry or user-visible recovery path.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: False success creates data and user-consistency failures.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Critical checkout should be protected, not shed first.

items.prompt: A team sizes a fleet using the average request rate and has no spare capacity for bursts. Which planning method is stronger?
constraints: The workload has bursty demand.
Latency objectives matter during the burst.
Historical metrics are available.

options.text: Use only the monthly average because averages remove measurement noise.
Size to the absolute theoretical maximum without considering cost or workload controls.
Use demand percentiles and burst duration, include scaling and recovery latency, preserve a defined headroom margin, and validate with load tests.
Use the smallest fleet and rely on users to retry during every burst.

feedback.Reason: Capacity planning must cover observed high-percentile demand and the time required to add capacity, not merely the average.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: Percentiles, burst duration, scale-out latency, and recovery demand convert workload measurements into an operational headroom target.
Details.scenarioApplication: The architect chooses a percentile aligned with the SLO, tests it under burst and failure conditions, and revisits the margin as traffic changes.
Details.errorCorrection: Averages hide bursts, unlimited maximum sizing is uneconomic and still needs testing, and user retries create additional load.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Higher headroom costs more, so the margin should be tied to an explicit availability and latency objective.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Averages conceal the high-demand intervals that cause saturation.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: Theoretical maximum is not a bounded business or capacity plan.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: User retries can amplify the burst and damage availability.

items.prompt: A production account's quota was lowered during an administrative change and the recovery plan no longer fits. Which control prevents a silent recurrence?
constraints: Quota values can change outside application deployment.
The recovery plan has explicit capacity assumptions.
The organization uses centralized operations.

options.text: Record the quota only in a wiki and review it annually.
Compare quota values with approved baselines, alert on drift, and make quota validation part of account and recovery readiness checks.
Remove the recovery plan so it cannot become inconsistent.
Ignore the quota because the application can retry failed launches forever.

feedback.Reason: Quota state is operational configuration and should be monitored against the assumptions used by the architecture.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A baseline and automated comparison expose quota drift before a recovery or launch event depends on it.
Details.scenarioApplication: The organization checks quotas in each target account and Region, alerts on material changes, and blocks readiness approval when headroom is missing.
Details.errorCorrection: Documentation alone becomes stale, deleting the recovery plan hides risk, and retries cannot bypass a quota.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Baselines need ownership and exception handling when demand or service limits change legitimately.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Annual documentation review is too slow for an operational quota dependency.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.C: Removing the plan does not remove the outage risk.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Retries remain subject to the same quota.

items.prompt: A recovery exercise launches the standby stack successfully but fails when traffic is restored because several API calls throttle. What should the exercise add?
constraints: The application has a tested standby deployment.
The restore path includes traffic and background jobs.
The throttled calls are retryable.

options.text: Declare recovery successful because the infrastructure stack reached CREATE_COMPLETE.
Increase retries until the exercise completes without recording quota usage.
Run the recovery test with production-like traffic, measure quota utilization and throttling, validate backoff and load shedding, and update headroom or quota requests from evidence.
Skip traffic restoration in future exercises because it is not part of infrastructure recovery.

feedback.Reason: Recovery validation must exercise the capacity and quota path that users depend on, not only resource creation.

Details.mechanismOrProperty: A successful infrastructure deployment does not prove API capacity, client retry behavior, or traffic restoration under recovery load.
Details.scenarioApplication: The team replays representative demand, observes quota and throttle metrics, validates bounded retries and load shedding, then fixes the recovery design.
Details.errorCorrection: CREATE_COMPLETE is not a service-level recovery result, unbounded retries hide the failure mode, and skipping traffic avoids the real test.
Details.boundaryOrTradeoff: Production-like tests need safety controls and scheduling, but without them the RTO and availability claims remain unverified.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.A: Infrastructure completion does not demonstrate serving capacity.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.B: More retries can conceal quota exhaustion and extend recovery time.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.D: Traffic restoration is part of the recovery outcome.
